claim: Cholinergic projections from the basal forebrain and brainstem are thought to play important roles in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and arousal.
source: Cholinergic projections from the basal forebrain and brainstem are thought to play important roles in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and arousal.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and consensus in the field.

claim: Optical stimulation of cholinergic inputs to the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) activates local GABAergic neurons to promote sleep and protect non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.
source: Using transgenic mice in which channelrhdopsin-2 is selectively expressed in cholinergic neurons, we show that optical stimulation of cholinergic inputs to the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) activates local GABAergic neurons to promote sleep and protect non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic mice experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Optical stimulation of cholinergic inputs to the TRN does not affect REM sleep.
source: It does not affect REM sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no changes in REM sleep duration.

claim: Direct activation of cholinergic input to the TRN shortens the time to sleep onset.
source: Instead, direct activation of cholinergic input to the TRN shortens the time to sleep onset and generates spindle oscillations that correlate with NREM sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of sleep onset latency in the study.

claim: Direct activation of cholinergic input to the TRN generates spindle oscillations that correlate with NREM sleep.
source: Instead, direct activation of cholinergic input to the TRN shortens the time to sleep onset and generates spindle oscillations that correlate with NREM sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing spindle oscillations and their correlation with NREM sleep.

claim: Cholinergic activation of the TRN evokes excitatory postsynaptic currents via α7-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: It does so by evoking excitatory postsynaptic currents via α7-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and inducing bursts of action potentials in local GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological experiments with specific receptor antagonists.

claim: Cholinergic activation of the TRN induces bursts of action potentials in local GABAergic neurons.
source: It does so by evoking excitatory postsynaptic currents via α7-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and inducing bursts of action potentials in local GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from GABAergic neurons in the TRN.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain and brainstem provide widespread projections to numerous brain regions, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, and TRN.
source: Cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain and brainstem provide widespread projections to numerous brain regions, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, and TRN (Mesulam et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Abundant behavioral and electrophysiological data suggest that cholinergic neurons play critical roles in regulating paradoxical sleep and the sleep-waking cycle.
source: Abundant behavioral and electrophysiological data suggest that cholinergic neurons play critical roles in regulating paradoxical sleep and the sleep-waking cycle (Koyama et al., 1994; Greco et al., 1999; Bellingham and Funk, 2000; Kobayashi et al., 2003; Boutrel and Koob, 2004; Darbra et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2012), as well as in promoting arousal.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Selective activation of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain induces immediate transition from sleep to waking.
source: Recently, it has been shown that selective activation of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain induces immediate transition from sleep to waking (Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The TRN serves as a gate for information flow between the cerebral cortex and thalamus due, in part, to its location near thalamic white matter and to the large numbers of GABAergic neurons it contains.
source: The TRN serves as a gate for information flow between the cerebral cortex and thalamus due, in part, to its location near thalamic white matter and to the large numbers of GABAergic neurons it contains (Houser et al., 1980; Pinault, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TRN is important for supporting attention.
source: The TRN is important for supporting attention (McAlonan et al., 2008), sleep regulation (Steriade et al., 1987; Espinosa et al., 2008), and sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Fogel and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The TRN is important for sleep regulation.
source: The TRN is important for supporting attention (McAlonan et al., 2008), sleep regulation (Steriade et al., 1987; Espinosa et al., 2008), and sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Fogel and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TRN is important for sleep-dependent memory consolidation.
source: The TRN is important for supporting attention (McAlonan et al., 2008), sleep regulation (Steriade et al., 1987; Espinosa et al., 2008), and sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Fogel and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Optical stimulation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN could induce spindle oscillations both in waking and sleep states.
source: We then tested EEG from the skull in vivo and found that optical stimulation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN could induce spindle oscillations both in waking and sleep states.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo EEG recordings from mice.

claim: EEG power increased with increasing stimulation intensity up to 200 ms pulse duration.
source: The visual inspection revealed increasing EEG power with increasing stimulation intensity. However, when the pulse intensity increased to 200 ms, the EEG power nearly reached the maximum (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of EEG power spectrograms shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The co-occurrence of spindle oscillation was greater during NREM than during the waking stage.
source: The co-occurrence of spindle oscillation was greater than that in the waking stage (P < 0.01; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of spindle co-occurrence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Spindle co-occurrence increased as the pulse duration increased.
source: Furthermore, spindle co-occurrence increased as the pulse duration increased (P < 0.01; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was no significant difference in co-occurrence between the 200 ms and 400 ms stimulation pulse-evoked spindle oscillations.
source: However, there was no significant difference in co-occurrence between the 200 ms and 400 ms stimulation pulse-evoked spindle oscillations (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was no significant difference in frequencies, amplitudes or durations between evoked and natural spindle oscillations.
source: Next, we compared the evoked and natural spindle oscillations and found there was no significant difference in their frequencies, amplitudes or durations (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of evoked and natural spindles shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The evoked spindle oscillation pattern mimicked the natural spindle oscillation pattern.
source: These results demonstrate that the evoked spindle oscillation pattern mimicked the natural spindle oscillation pattern.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison data showing no significant differences between evoked and natural spindles.

claim: A light pulse with a 6 s interval evoked the highest spindle oscillation densities in both waking and NREM phases.
source: We then quantified the spindle density and found that the light pulse with a 6 s interval evoked the highest spindle oscillation densities in both waking and NREM phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of spindle density under different stimulation intervals.

claim: The evoked spindle density was 9.2 ± 0.5 per min in the NREM stage with a 6 s interval light pulse.
source: The evoked spindle density was 9.2 ± 0.5 per min in the NREM stage with a 6 s interval light pulse.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurement of spindle density.

claim: The stimulation protocol induced sleep onset in ChAT-ChR2 mice within 16 min, on average.
source: The stimulation protocol induced sleep onset in ChAT-ChR2 mice (ChAT-ChR2-Sti) within 16 min, on average (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of sleep onset latency shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: Optical stimulation shortened sleep onset by 50-60% compared to controls.
source: This was 50–60% quicker (P < 0.05) than in ChAT-ChR2 mice without stimulation (ChAT-ChR2-NonSti) and in WT mice with stimulation (WT-Sti).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of sleep onset times between groups.

claim: There was no significant difference in sleep onset between WT-Sti mice and ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice.
source: There was no significant difference between WT-Sti mice and ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (P = 0.49).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison showing p=0.49.

claim: The shortened sleep onset was mediated by ChR2-induced activation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN.
source: These results suggest that the shortened sleep onset was mediated by ChR2-induced activation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between ChAT-ChR2 mice with stimulation versus controls.

claim: The total sleep time of ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice stimulated for 1 hr increased significantly compared with that of both ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice and WT-Sti mice.
source: Correspondingly, the total sleep time of ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice stimulated for 1 hr increased significantly compared with that of both ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (P < 0.01) and WT-Sti mice (P < 0.01) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of total sleep time shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Time spent in NREM sleep in ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice increased by 160% compared with that of ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice.
source: Time spent in NREM sleep in ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice increased by 160% compared with that of ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (P < 0.01), while no difference was seen in the duration of REM sleep (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of sleep architecture shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No difference was seen in the duration of REM sleep between ChAT-ChR2-Sti and ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice.
source: Time spent in NREM sleep in ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice increased by 160% compared with that of ChAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (P < 0.01), while no difference was seen in the duration of REM sleep (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: It took an average of 40 ± 3 min to recover normal function following cessation of stimulation.
source: To test how long it took for recovery of normal function, we recorded sleep states for 1 hr following cessation of stimulation, and found that it took an average of 40 ± 3 min to recover (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of recovery time shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN can promote sleep onset and alter sleep architecture to protect sleep.
source: These results suggest that activation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN can promote sleep onset and alter sleep architecture to protect sleep.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing shortened sleep onset and increased NREM sleep.

claim: Spindle oscillations can protect and stabilize sleep.
source: Previous studies revealed that spindle oscillations can protect and stabilize sleep (Bové et al., 1994; Dang-Vu et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spindle density in ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice was significantly increased compared with that of ChAT-ChR2-NonSti and WT-Sti mice.
source: Spindle density in ChAT-ChR2-Sti mice was significantly increased compared with that of ChAT-ChR2-NonSti and WT-Sti mice, while no differences were seen between ChAT-ChR2-NonSti and WT-Sti mice (p< 0.01, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Spindle density was greatest (9.3 ± 0.5 min) during NREM sleep in all three groups.
source: In all three groups, spindle density was greatest (9.3 ± 0.5 min) during NREM sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurement of spindle density across sleep states.

claim: There is a significant positive relationship between spindle oscillation density and NREM sleep duration.
source: Correlation analysis indicated a significant positive relationship between spindle oscillation density and NREM sleep duration (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Evoked spindle oscillations can play roles similar to those of spontaneous spindle oscillations in protecting and stabilizing sleep.
source: These results suggest that evoked spindle oscillations can play roles similar to those of spontaneous spindle oscillations in protecting and stabilizing sleep.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between evoked spindles and NREM sleep duration.

claim: The TRN consists of a homogenous population of parvalbumin (PV)-containing GABAergic neurons.
source: The TRN is thought to represent a shield surrounding the dorsal thalamus consisting of a homogenous population of parvalbumin (PV)-containing GABAergic neurons (Houser et al., 1980; Ohara and Lieberman, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PV-positive neurons were abundant throughout the TRN.
source: Confocal imaging of brain slices from B13 mice (which express GFP under a PV promoter) after immunostaining for PV confirmed that PV-positive neurons were abundant throughout the TRN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Numerous cholinergic fibers surround PV-positive neurons in the TRN of ChAT-ChR2 mice.
source: Immunostaining revealed numerous cholinergic fibers surrounding PV-positive neurons in the TRN of ChAT-ChR2 mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A 5-ms pulse could induce the firing of action potentials in cholinergic neurons when stimulating cell bodies.
source: First, we stimulated cholinergic neurons and found that a 5-ms pulse could induce the firing of action potentials in the cholinergic neurons when stimulating cell bodies (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Light pulses of short duration (5 ms and 50 ms) failed to induce bursts of action potentials in GABAergic neurons.
source: We found that light pulses of short duration, such as 5 ms and 50 ms, failed to induce bursts of action potentials in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from GABAergic neurons.

claim: A light pulse of at least 100 ms was required to induce bursts of action potentials and spindles.
source: A light pulse of at least 100 ms was required to induce bursts of action potentials and spindles.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings testing different pulse durations.

claim: A 200-ms light pulse evoked fast excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) in PV neurons in the TRN.
source: Whole-cell recording in voltage-clamp mode from PV neurons in the TRN-containing brain slice showed that pure light stimulation (without injection current) of a 200-ms pulse evoked fast excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs; Figure 4E, lower).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs were accompanied by rhythmic high-frequency bursts of action potentials in PV neurons.
source: They were accompanied by rhythmic high-frequency bursts of action potentials (APs) seen in current-clamp mode (Figure 4E, upper).
evidence: This claim is supported by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Optical stimulation of cholinergic fibers induced spikes in GABAergic neurons in vivo in anesthetized ChAT-ChR2 mice.
source: In vivo extracellular recording in the TRN of anesthetized ChAT-ChR2 mice revealed that the optical stimulation of cholinergic fibers induced spikes in the GABAergic neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Cholinergic projections to the TRN produce excitatory input sufficient to evoke bursts of APs in PV-containing TRN neurons.
source: These results suggest that cholinergic projections to the TRN produce excitatory input sufficient to evoke bursts of APs in PV-containing TRN neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiological recordings showing EPSCs and action potential bursts.

claim: The DsRed signal was detected in some cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (nBM) in the basal forebrain.
source: We found that the DsRed signal was detected in some cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (nBM) in the basal forebrain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) of the brain stem (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The DsRed signal was detected in some cholinergic neurons of the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) of the brain stem.
source: We found that the DsRed signal was detected in some cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (nBM) in the basal forebrain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) of the brain stem (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: About 30% of cholinergic neurons were positive for mCherry in the nBM.
source: Statistical results showed that about 30% of cholinergic neurons (VAChT antibody labeled) were positive for mCherry (retrograde virus labeled) in the nBM, and ~7% were positive for mCherry in the PPTg (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of retrograde labeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: About 7% of cholinergic neurons were positive for mCherry in the PPTg.
source: Statistical results showed that about 30% of cholinergic neurons (VAChT antibody labeled) were positive for mCherry (retrograde virus labeled) in the nBM, and ~7% were positive for mCherry in the PPTg (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of retrograde labeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRN neurons receive cholinergic projections from both the basal forebrain and brain stem.
source: These results demonstrate that TRN neurons receive cholinergic projections from both the basal forebrain and brain stem.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the retrograde tracing results showing labeled neurons in both nBM and PPTg.

claim: TTX completely prevented optical stimulation of cholinergic fibers from eliciting EPSCs in PV-containing neurons.
source: Recordings in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM) to block APs completely prevented optical stimulation of cholinergic fibers in the TRN of ChAT-ChR2 mice from eliciting EPSCs in PV-containing neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The light-evoked EPSCs are AP-dependent, as expected for presynaptic stimulation of transmitter release.
source: This is consistent with the EPSCs being AP-dependent, as expected for presynaptic stimulation of transmitter release.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TTX blocking experiment.

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs were not blocked by the combination of CNQX, AP5, and picrotoxin.
source: In contrast, light-evoked EPSCs were not blocked by including the combination of CNQX (20 μM) as an inhibitor of glutamatergic AMPA receptors, AP5 (50 μM) as an inhibitor of glutamatergic NMDA receptors, and picrotoxin (PTX, 100 μM) as an inhibitor of GABAA receptors (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neither rapid glutamatergic nor GABAergic transmission is required for cholinergic induction of the EPSCs.
source: This indicates that neither rapid glutamatergic nor GABAergic transmission is required for cholinergic induction of the EPSCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure of glutamatergic and GABAergic receptor blockers to prevent EPSCs.

claim: Dihydro-β-erythroidine (DHβE) decreased the amplitude of light-evoked EPSCs by 12%, 34%, and 99% at 5 nM, 10 nM, and 100 nM, respectively.
source: Dihydro-β-erythroidine (DHβE), a selective antagonist of α4β2-containing nAChRs, decreased the amplitude of light-evoked EPSCs by 12%, 34%, and 99% at 5 nM, 10 nM, and 100 nM, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Methyllycaconitine (MLA, 5 nM) completely blocked the light-evoked EPSCs.
source: However, methyllycaconitine (MLA, 5 nM), a specific antagonist of α7-nAChRs, completely blocked the light-evoked EPSCs (Figure 5D) and the accompanying bursts of APs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MLA (5 nM) completely blocked the accompanying bursts of APs.
source: However, methyllycaconitine (MLA, 5 nM), a specific antagonist of α7-nAChRs, completely blocked the light-evoked EPSCs (Figure 5D) and the accompanying bursts of APs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The concentration of MLA used (5 nM) was consistent with previous research.
source: The concentration was consistent with previous research (Bonfante-Cabarcas et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Immunostaining yielded extensive labeling for α7-nAChRs on PV-containing neurons in the TRN.
source: Immunostaining yielded extensive labeling for α7-nAChRs on PV-containing neurons in the TRN (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The light-evoked, AP-dependent release of ACh from cholinergic projections in the TRN elicits EPSCs and bursts of APs in GABAergic neurons of the TRN by activating α7-nAChRs.
source: These results indicate that the light-evoked, AP-dependent release of ACh from cholinergic projections in the TRN elicits EPSCs and bursts of APs in GABAergic neurons of the TRN by activating α7-nAChRs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined pharmacological and electrophysiological experiments.

claim: MLA completely blocked light-evoked changes in latency to sleep onset, total sleep time, and sleep architecture.
source: Quantification of the responses indicated that MLA completely blocked light-evoked changes in latency to sleep onset, total sleep time, and sleep architecture (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments with MLA injection shown in Figure 6.

claim: Saline-injected mice could still be induced to sleep and showed increased NREM by the activation of cholinergic fibers during the 1 hr stimulation.
source: In contrast, the saline-injected mice could still be induced to sleep and showed increased NREM by the activation of cholinergic fibers during the 1 hr stimulation, compared with the ChAT-ChR2-Sti-MLA and WT-Sti groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of saline-injected mice with MLA-injected and control mice.

claim: In vivo injection of MLA significantly decreased spontaneous sleep time from 37.2 ± 4.1 min to 27.3 ± 3.2 min.
source: To further test MLA on spontaneous sleep, we injected saline and MLA into the TRN of ChAT-ChR2 mice in the daytime, and found that in vivo injection of MLA (the antagonist of α7-nAChRs) significantly decreased spontaneous sleep time from 37.2 ± 4.1 min to 27.3 ± 3.2 min (p < 0.01, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of spontaneous sleep time shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cholinergic promotion of sleep onset and sleep protection are mediated by activating PV-expressing neurons of the TRN through α7-nAChRs.
source: These results indicate that cholinergic promotion of sleep onset and sleep protection are mediated by activating PV-expressing neurons of the TRN through α7-nAChRs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the MLA blocking experiments showing that α7-nAChR antagonism prevents sleep-promoting effects.

claim: A light pulse of 10 ms applied to an acute slice could induce bursts of APs in GABAergic neurons of the TRN.
source: Testing the paradigm first in vitro showed that a light pulse of 10 ms applied to an acute slice could induce bursts of APs in GABAergic neurons of the TRN (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 8 Hz stimulation was most successful at evoking spindle oscillations both in waking and NREM states.
source: Testing three different optical stimulation patterns in vivo (20 Hz, 8 Hz, or single 10 ms pulses) indicated that 8 Hz stimulation was most successful at evoking spindle oscillations both in waking and NREM states (P < 0.05, Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of different stimulation frequencies shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Optical stimulation significantly reduced the sleep onset time of VGAT-ChR2 mice (VGAT-ChR2-Sti, 27.2 ± 3.2 min) compared with that of the controls (VGAT-ChR2-NonSti; 5.5 ± 0.8 min).
source: Optical stimulation significantly reduced the sleep onset time of VGAT-ChR2 mice (VGAT-ChR2-Sti, 27.2 ± 3.2 min) compared with that of the controls (VGAT-ChR2-NonSti; 5.5 ± 0.8 min, P < 0.01, Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of sleep onset time shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The duration of sleep during the 1 hr optical stimulation period increased by 156% compared with that of the controls.
source: Similarly, the duration of sleep during the 1 hr optical stimulation period also increased by 156% compared with that of the controls (P < 0.01, Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of total sleep time shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Time spent in the NREM phase was significantly greater for VGAT-ChR2-Sti mice (27.2 ± 2.1 min) than for VGAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (15.2 ± 1.3 min).
source: Time spent in the NREM phase was significantly greater for VGAT-ChR2-Sti mice (27.2 ± 2.1 min) than for VGAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (15.2 ± 1.3 min, p < 0.01), while no significant differences were seen in the duration of the REM stage (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement of sleep architecture shown in Figure 7G.

claim: No significant differences were seen in the duration of the REM stage between VGAT-ChR2-Sti and VGAT-ChR2-NonSti mice.
source: Time spent in the NREM phase was significantly greater for VGAT-ChR2-Sti mice (27.2 ± 2.1 min) than for VGAT-ChR2-NonSti mice (15.2 ± 1.3 min, p < 0.01), while no significant differences were seen in the duration of the REM stage (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Elevating the activity of GABAergic neurons in the TRN can promote sleep in ways that mimic the effects of cholinergic excitation of the TRN.
source: These results support that elevating the activity of GABAergic neurons in the TRN can promote sleep in ways that mimic the effects of cholinergic excitation of the TRN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of effects between direct GABAergic stimulation and cholinergic stimulation.

claim: Cholinergic projections to the TRN can activate local GABAergic neurons via α7-nAChRs without requiring either glutamatergic or GABAergic rapid transmission.
source: Our results show that cholinergic projections to the TRN can activate local GABAergic neurons via α7-nAChRs without requiring either glutamatergic or GABAergic rapid transmission.
evidence: This claim summarizes the mechanistic findings from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Cholinergic fiber activation of GABAergic neurons in the TRN in vivo can promote sleep onset and increase the probability of spindle oscillation and duration of the NREM phase.
source: Furthermore, cholinergic fiber activation of GABAergic neurons in the TRN in vivo can promote sleep onset and increase the probability of spindle oscillation and duration of the NREM phase.
evidence: This claim summarizes the behavioral findings from the in vivo experiments.

claim: Direct stimulation of GABAergic neurons in the TRN to elicit activity comparable to that induced by cholinergic input produces the same kinds of changes in sleep behavior seen following cholinergic activation of the neurons.
source: Lastly, direct stimulation of GABAergic neurons in the TRN to elicit activity comparable to that induced by cholinergic input produces the same kinds of changes in sleep behavior seen following cholinergic activation of the neurons.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from VGAT-ChR2 experiments.

claim: Cholinergic input, acting through GABAergic neurons in the TRN, can promote critical features of sleep.
source: These results demonstrate the capacity of cholinergic input, acting through GABAergic neurons in the TRN, to promote critical features of sleep.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion inferred from all the experimental results.

claim: Previous studies employing pharmacology, brain injury, and electrical stimulation revealed important contributions of cholinergic signaling to the regulation of the sleep-to-waking cycle and paradoxical sleep.
source: Previous studies employing pharmacology, brain injury, and electrical stimulation revealed important contributions of cholinergic signaling to the regulation of the sleep-to-waking cycle and paradoxical sleep (Campbell et al., 1969; Sarter et al., 2009; Brown et al., 2012; Hamlin et al., 2013; Sims et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Earlier studies suggested that cholinergic input to the TRN neurons was primarily inhibitory, acting on M2 muscarinic ACh receptors.
source: These earlier studies suggested that cholinergic input to the TRN neurons was primarily inhibitory, acting on M2 muscarinic ACh receptors (McCormick and Prince, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Local delivery of ACh to the TRN was seen to induce only a slow inhibitory response, leading to the conclusion that the ACh-induced bursts of APs observed were somehow the result of the GABAergic neurons in the TRN becoming hyperpolarized.
source: Local delivery of ACh to the TRN was seen to induce only a slow inhibitory response, leading to the conclusion that the ACh-induced bursts of APs observed were somehow the result of the GABAergic neurons in the TRN becoming hyperpolarized (McCormick and Prince, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous failures to detect an α7-nAChR response in the TRN were almost certainly caused by electrical stimulation methods, i.e. ACh perfusion.
source: Previous failures to detect an α7-nAChR response in the TRN were almost certainly caused by electrical stimulation methods, i.e. ACh perfusion.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about why previous studies did not detect α7-nAChR responses.

claim: α7-nAChRs desensitize so quickly that their responses can be missed in experimental paradigms.
source: Because α7-nAChRs desensitize so quickly (Giniatullin et al., 2005), their responses can be missed in experimental paradigms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research about α7-nAChR desensitization.

claim: EPSPs induced by electrical stimulation were blocked by dihydro-β-erythroidine (DhβE, 300 nM), indicating that the EPSPs were mediated by α4β2-containing nAChRs.
source: Another group found that Excitatory Postsynaptic Potentials (EPSPs) induced by electrical stimulation were blocked by dihydro-β-erythroidine (DhβE, 300 nM), indicating that the EPSPs were mediated by α4β2-containing nAChRs (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: DhβE (300 nM) can block both α4β2- and α7 nAChR-mediated currents.
source: However, DhβE (300 nM) can block both α4β2- and α7 nAChR-mediated currents (Alkondon and Albuquerque, 1993), and non-specific electrical stimulation may enable extrasynaptic transmitter release.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain send projections to many targets, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, and TRN.
source: Cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain send projections to many targets, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, and TRN.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Selective activation of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain has been shown to induce an immediate transition from sleep to waking.
source: Selective activation of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain has been shown to induce an immediate transition from sleep to waking (Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Specific activation of cholinergic fibers locally in the TRN showed the opposite effect to basal forebrain activation, inducing transition from waking to sleep.
source: The present study specifically activated cholinergic fibers locally in the TRN, which, surprisingly, showed the opposite effect. It induced transition from waking to sleep, indicating that direct cholinergic projections to the TRN promote sleep onset and sleep stabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the present study.

claim: GABAergic neurons of the TRN fire AP bursts mediating slow and spindle waves.

claim: AP bursts in TRN neurons are very important for the generation of thalamocortical spindle waves.
source: These bursts are very important for the generation of thalamocortical spindle waves (von Krosigk et al., 1993; Lee et al., 2013), and spindle rhythms play important roles in protecting sleep initiation and elevating arousal threshold (Steriade, 2005; Wimmer et al., 2012).
